Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Assess the etiology and epidemiology of meniscal tears in young patients.
Interpret the pathoanatomy of discoid lateral menisci.
Review surgical treatment options and techniques for meniscal repair.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Acute injuries to the meniscus often result from twisting events during loading of the knee.
The meniscus functions as a shock absorber between the femur and tibia and relies on intact
circumferentially oriented fibers to absorb force and convert axial loads to hoop stresses,
protecting the articular cartilage from abnormal wear.
Vascular supply is from the periphery. The outer third of the meniscus is termed red-red zone
because of abundant blood supply, the middle third is the red-white zone, and the inner third

is the white-white zone because of poor vascularity.
Tear location and pattern have implications for the success of repair or nonsurgical
management attempts. Tears occurring close to the vascular zone are associated with the
highest rates of successful healing.
Discoid meniscus refers to an abnormally large meniscus that does not have the usual
contour. Discoid menisci also have an inherently different microstructure and may have
abnormal peripheral attachments. This may result in an increased risk for tearing and
instability of the meniscus. They are traditionally classified as partial, complete, or Wrisberg
variant (Figure 1). A newer arthroscopic classification relies on features of the discoid
meniscus including meniscal width, meniscal height, peripheral stability, and meniscal tear.1
Figure 1 Illustrations show the classification system for lateral discoid menisci. A, Type I
(complete). B, Type II (incomplete). C, Type III (Wrisberg ligament). Type III discoid menisci have
no posterior attachment to the tibia. The only posterior attachment is through the ligament of
Wrisberg toward the medial femoral condyle. (Reproduced with permission from
Neuschwander DC: Discoid lateral meniscus, in Fu FH, Harner CD, Vince KG, eds: Knee Surgery.
Baltimore, MD, Williams and Wilkins, 1994, p 394.)

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The meniscus is a semilunar cartilage structure in the medial and lateral compartments
of the knee that cover one-half to one-third of the tibial plateau surface area. The

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001056

meniscus appears triangular in cross section in both the sagittal and coronal planes,
particularly on MRI. The meniscus functions as a shock absorber between the femur and
tibia and relies on intact circumferentially oriented fibers to absorb axial forces,
converting them to and hoop stresses. The meniscal vascular supply is from its
periphery, and the outer third of the meniscus is termed the red-red zone because of
abundant blood supply. The middle third is the red-white zone, and the inner third is the
white-white zone because of lack of vascularity. The vascular supply is critical to the
ability of the meniscus to heal after a tear and/or repair. Pediatric/adolescent menisci
are thought to have better ability to heal after repair compared with adult menisci
because of comparably better vascular supply. Tear location and pattern have
implications for the success of repair or nonsurgical management attempts. Tears that
occur close to the periphery are associated with the highest rates of successful
outcomes.
A unique anatomic variant of the meniscus is called a discoid meniscus. This variant is
almost exclusively found in the lateral meniscus; however, scattered case reports of
discoid medial menisci exist. Discoid meniscus refers to an abnormally large meniscus
that does not have the usual contour. Discoid menisci also have an inherently different
microstructure and may have abnormal peripheral attachments. This may result in an
increased risk for tears and instability of the meniscus. Discoid menisci are traditionally
classified as partial, complete, or Wrisberg variant (Figure 1).
Epidemiology
Discoid lateral meniscus has an incidence of 3.2 per 100,000 person-years, with 12.6% of
individuals having bilateral symptomatic discoid menisci2 (Resource 1).
Non-discoid meniscus tears are more commonly associated with concurrent ligament injury,
particularly anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears.
Ellis et al3 reported that 97% of lateral meniscus pathology in patients younger than 13 years
was associated with a discoid lateral meniscus and 59% of lateral meniscus pathology in
patients aged 14 to 16 years was associated with a discoid lateral meniscus.


Epidemiology
Meniscal tears are quite common in the adult population and are less common
comparatively in the pediatric and adolescent populations; however, they are not rare.
Non-discoid meniscus tears are more commonly associated with concurrent ligament
injury, particularly ACL tears. In general, lateral meniscus tears are associated with acute
ACL tears, and medial meniscus tears tend to be associated with chronic ACL deficiency;
however, these are not exclusive findings, and acute ACL tears may be associated with
lateral and medial meniscus tears. Discoid lateral meniscus is associated with an
incidence of 3.2 per 100,000 person-years, with 12.6% of individuals having bilateral
symptomatic discoid menisci.2
Discoid lateral meniscus tears may be associated with trauma and sports activities but
also may be associated with atraumatic mechanisms of injury. Ellis et al3 reported that
97% and 59% of lateral meniscus pathology in patients younger than 13 years and
patients aged 14 to 16 years, respectively, was associated with a discoid lateral
meniscus. The younger the patient with a torn lateral meniscus, the more likely the
meniscus is a discoid variant.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Joints and Ligaments
Normal lateral meniscus is more circular and more mobile than the medial meniscus.
The medial meniscus is more C-shaped and has more firm peripheral attachments than the
lateral meniscus.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Menisci are crescent-shaped and composed of dense, tightly woven collagen fibers. Their
structure and collagen arrangement allows for elasticity and the ability to withstand
compressive forces during weight bearing. The lateral meniscus is more circular in form

9/3/26, 4:42 PM
AAOS | Meniscal Tears and Discoid Meniscus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001056
4/28

and can cover up to two-thirds of the articular surface of the tibial plateau in a normal
meniscus and can cover the entire articular surface in a discoid lateral meniscus. The
lateral meniscus is more mobile, thicker around its periphery, and wider in the body but
smaller in diameter than the medial meniscus. In addition to the lateral meniscal root
attachments, the lateral meniscus often is anchored to the femur by the ligament of
Humphrey and Wrisberg.
The medial meniscus is more C-shaped than the circular lateral meniscus, with its
posterior horn being wider than its anterior horn. The peripheral aspect of the medial
meniscus is firmly attached to the medial capsule and the deep portion of the medial
collateral ligament. The coronary ligaments attach the medial meniscus to the tibial
plateau.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The meniscus rapidly loses its vascularity early in life. Pediatric menisci still have more
vascularity than adult menisci.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The newborn meniscus is completely vascularized at birth, but the central third quickly
loses that vascularity by age 9 months. By age 10 years, the vascularity is limited to the
peripheral 10% to 30%. The limited vascularity is a potential etiology of meniscal injury
and also a limitation in the ability of the meniscus to heal from these injuries. Children
have increased vascularity of their menisci compared with adults and, therefore, have
increased propensity to heal after surgical repair of the menisci compared with adults.
In general, non-discoid meniscus tears are associated with trauma in young patients.
These are commonly associated with ligament injuries, especially ACL tears. Lateral
meniscus tears are more commonly associated with an acute ACL tear, whereas medial
meniscus tears are more associated with chronic ACL insufficiency.

Risk Factors
The major risk factors for meniscal tear in young patients are concomitant ligament injury
(especially ACL tears) and discoid lateral meniscus morphology.
With discoid meniscus, adults are more likely to present with a tear compared to pediatric
patients. Pediatric patients are more likely to have a horizontal tear pattern while adults are
more likely to have a complex tear pattern in discoid lateral meniscus.4
Discoid lateral meniscus is more common in pediatric patients with Asian and/or
Hispanic/Latino ethnicity.5
Associated Injuries
Concomitant ligament injury, especially ACL tears, often are associated with non-discoid
meniscus tears in children.

Associated Injuries
Meniscal injury can occur in isolation but also often is associated with concomitant
ligamentous injury. Isolated lateral meniscal injury in a young child often is associated
with discoid meniscus morphology. Peripheral posterior horn lateral meniscus tears
often are associated with acute ACL tears. Peripheral posterior medial meniscus tears
often are associated with more chronic ACL deficiency (often referred to as ramp
lesions).
Injury Classification
Meniscal tears are classified descriptively.
Location of tear: red-red zone, vascular, outer third; red-white zone, middle third; white zone,
avascular, inner third
Size/length of tear
Pattern of tear: horizontal, vertical, radial, bucket-handle, parrot beak, complex, or
combination (Figure 2; Resource 2).

Mechanism of Injury

Mechanism of Injury
Although specific patterns of meniscal injury can occur from various mechanisms of
injury, longitudinal peripheral tears in the red-red or red-white zones often are
associated with ACL tears, particularly in the lateral meniscus. Further propagation of a
longitudinal peripheral tear may result in a bucket-handle tear of the meniscus.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Meniscal tears can occur after a traumatic or atraumatic event. In general, an axial load
simultaneously occurs with flexion or twisting of the knee.
Young children with discoid menisci may present with an insidious onset.
Patients with discoid meniscus may have locking (33%) and snapping (30%).6
Patients may report a pop followed by pain and swelling.
Some children may report a history of atraumatic mechanical symptoms, including locking,
catching, or popping, especially laterally; this may indicate the presence of a discoid lateral
meniscus.
Other symptoms that are associated with discoid lateral menisci include painless loss of
extension and reproducible snapping.

Patient History
Evaluation of a patient in whom a meniscal tear is suspected always begins with a
thorough patient history. Some children may report a history of atraumatic mechanical
symptoms, including locking, catching, or popping, especially laterally; this may indicate
a discoid lateral meniscus. Other symptoms that are associated with discoid lateral
menisci include painless loss of extension and reproducible snapping. Many children will
report pain as the primary symptom of a meniscal tear; however, knee swelling and/or
mechanical symptoms also should prompt additional evaluation for a meniscal tear.

Meniscal tears can occur after a traumatic or atraumatic event. In general, an axial load
simultaneously occurs with flexion or twisting of the knee. Patients may report a pop
followed by pain and swelling; however, the pop also may be a sign of an ACL tear.
Physical Examination
Physical examination has good sensitivity and excellent specificity for medial meniscus
pathology.7
Effusion may be present.
Range of motion may be limited because of effusion, pain, or mechanical block.
Asymmetric deficit of knee flexion may indicate a discoid lateral meniscus, particularly a
discoid meniscus with anterior detachment and posterior displacement.8
Point tenderness at the joint line
Provocative testing, including hyperflexion, the McMurray test, the Apley test, and the Thessaly
test, which may produce pain and a pop.
Examination of the knee ligaments is important because of the potential for concomitant
injury.

Physical Examination
A detailed physical examination of the knee can aid in the diagnosis of meniscal
pathology and associated ligamentous injury. Knee effusions are a very sensitive sign for
intra-articular pathology. Joint line tenderness often is present in patients with a
meniscal tear. Inability to fully extend the knee is particularly concerning for a displaced
meniscal fragment, especially a bucket-handle tear. Various provocative tests, including
hyperflexion, the McMurray test, the Apley test, and the Thessaly test, can help
distinguish meniscal pathology from other knee conditions. Examination of ligamentous
stability should include, at a minimum, varus and valgus testing in full extension and in
30° of flexion, the anterior and posterior drawer tests, the Lachman test, and the dial
test in 30° and 90° of flexion.

Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs may appear normal; however, they may indicate a discoid lateral meniscus with a
widened lateral joint line, lateral femoral condyle flattening, and high fibular head height.9,10
Patella alta may be an independent risk factor for isolated meniscus tears in skeletally
immature patients.11
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is indicated to evaluate the knee for a discoid meniscus, meniscal tears, and other intra-
articular diagnoses, especially concomitant ligament injury.
MRI results in a high false-positive rate in children younger than 10 years because of the
abundant vascularity of the meniscus in this age group, which may appear similar to a tear.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Imaging of the injured knee in a child should always include radiographs to evaluate/rule
out fracture or bony abnormalities, such as osteochondritis dissecans. Most radiographs
should be negative in an otherwise normal pediatric or adolescent patient with a
meniscal tear. Discoid lateral menisci with or without a tear are associated with a
widened lateral joint line, lateral femoral condyle flattening, and high fibular head height.
Negative radiographs in a child with a painful swollen knee, particularly with mechanical
symptoms, usually prompts additional evaluation via MRI. MRI is indicated to evaluate
the knee for a discoid meniscus, meniscal tears, and other intra-articular diagnoses,
especially concomitant ligament injury; however, MRI is associated with in a high false-
positive rate in children younger than 10 years because of the abundant vascularity of
the meniscus in this age group, which may appear similar to a tear.
Preoperative MRI of discoid meniscal instability continues to evolve. The phantom sign is
defined as an abnormal signal intensity observed at the anterior tibial insertion of the
ACL on coronal MRIs of the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus.12

Discoid lateral meniscus is associated with other bony morphologic changes observed
on MRIs, including larger bicondylar width and notch width, larger tibial plateau width,
and smaller lateral and coronal tibial slopes.13
Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for knee pain, swelling, and/or mechanical symptoms in a child, in
addition to meniscal tear, includes ligament injury, osteochondral fracture, osteochondritis
dissecans, and patellar instability.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
The management of incidentally noted, asymptomatic discoid menisci involves observation.
Small peripheral or incomplete tears (5 mm or less, in the red-red zone) may heal or become
asymptomatic with nonsurgical management.
Rest, with or without bracing, to limit range of motion to 90° of knee flexion for 4 to 6 weeks
followed by physical therapy to regain strength and range of motion
NSAIDs and icing may be used as an adjuvant treatment option.
After pain and swelling have subsided, range of motion and strength must be returned to
preinjury level.
If no new symptoms (including swelling, pain, or mechanical symptoms) are present and
range of motion and strength have been restored, then progression back to sports and
activities can be initiated.

Nonsurgical Management
Because the risk of further tear propagation may be high in this patient population,
experience and literature supporting nonsurgical management is limited. In general,
rest, ice, NSAIDs, and activity modifications in combination with lower extremity
rehabilitation may allow for healing of small, nondisplaced tears in the vascular zone of
the meniscus. After swelling and pain have diminished, strengthening and sport-specific

training is possible. If a pediatric patient is unable to progress with rehabilitation
because of continued knee pain, swelling, or mechanical symptoms, surgical treatment
should be considered.
Discoid meniscus pathology can be managed nonsurgically in patients with minimal
symptoms (swelling, mechanical symptoms) or in patients with a discoid meniscus found
incidentally who are asymptomatic. Rest, NSAIDs, and rehabilitation may allow these
children to return to normal activities; however, surgical treatment should be considered
if patients are unable to progress with rehabilitation because of continued knee pain,
swelling, or mechanical symptoms.
For patients initially treated nonsurgically or for discoid menisci that are diagnosed
incidentally in asymptomatic patients, close follow-up and observation is imperative
because of the substantial risk of asymptomatic discoid menisci progressing to a
symptomatic tear.
Surgical Management
Indications
Mechanical symptoms, bucket-handle tears, meniscal root tears, meniscal tears causing
extrusion of the meniscus or loss of circumferential fiber integrity, discoid meniscus tears, and
associated ligament injury (Video 1)
Failed nonsurgical management with persistent pain

Outside-In, and Root Repair) [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2017. https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/18324__Videos. Accessed March 16, 2021.

Indications
Indications for the surgical management of a meniscal tear in a pediatric/adolescent
patient should be broader than in adult patients given the risk of long-term arthrosis if
meniscal tissue is not preserved and the improved proclivity for meniscal healing after
repair in younger patients. Surgical management should be considered in patients with
mechanical symptoms, bucket-handle tears, meniscal root tears, meniscal tears causing
extrusion of the meniscus or loss of circumferential fiber integrity, discoid meniscus
tears, and associated ligament injuries. Surgical treatment also should be offered to
patients with persistent pain or swelling/mechanical symptoms and imaging studies
consistent with a meniscal tear in whom nonsurgical treatment fails. Meniscal injury in
patients with another ligamentous injury (particularly an ACL injury) should be managed
at time of surgery. Some indications and surgeon preference exist for staged treatment
of some patients with a concomitant meniscal and ligamentous injury. In these patients,
meniscal repair generally is performed first (ie, bucket-handle repair of the meniscus),
with staged reconstruction of the ACL and/or other ligaments after swelling has

management of these concomitant injuries may be considered; however, many surgeons
prefer to manage meniscal and ligament injuries at the same time.
Techniques/Procedures
Partial meniscectomy is reserved for irreparable tears or small tears in the white-white zone.
(Video 2).
Saucerization of a torn discoid meniscus with repair of remaining torn meniscal tissue.
Preservation of a rim that is 10 mm wide during saucerization is associated with good
outcomes.
Meniscal repair is the preferred treatment option for pediatric and adolescent patients if the
tear pattern and condition of the meniscal tissue is appropriate for repair.

Preoperative Planning
Preoperative imaging studies, including MRI, are essential for surgical management.

Preoperative Planning
Although MRI may not be able to fully elucidate repairable versus irreparable tear
patterns, the presence of bucket-handle or meniscal root tear patterns may alert the
surgical team to the need for additional surgical instrumentation and preparation.
Patient Positioning
Standard supine knee arthroscopy positioning is recommended.
A circumferential arthroscopy leg holder may be useful for additional valgus stress, particularly
with posterior medial meniscus pathology access.
Figure-of-four leg positioning for lateral joint exposure is standard for lateral meniscus
pathology.
Surgical Approaches
Diagnostic arthroscopy is performed first to evaluate the repairability of the meniscus and
assess for other intra-articular pathology.

Surgical Approaches
Diagnostic arthroscopy is performed first to evaluate the repairability of the meniscus
and assess for other intra-articular pathology. In general, diagnostic arthroscopy is
performed via anterolateral and anteromedial portals. Partial meniscectomy and all-
inside meniscus repair techniques generally can be performed via these arthroscopy
portals alone. If partial meniscectomy is performed in patients with a discoid lateral
meniscus, better outcomes have been observed with preservation of at least 10 mm of
meniscus width.14 (Figure 3)

Figure 3 Arthroscopic images show saucerization of a discoid lateral meniscus. A basket
(A) and a shaver (B) are used to create a normal C-shaped meniscus. (Reproduced from
Mehta P, Brafman RT, Ahmad CS: Evaluation and management of discoid meniscus, in
Ahmad CS, ed: Pediatric and Adolescent Sports Injuries. Rosemont, IL, American Academy

If inside-out meniscal repair is indicated, then posteromedial or posterolateral
exposures can be used for medial or lateral meniscus repairs, respectively (Video 3).
Posteromedial dissection involves careful superficial dissection to avoid the saphenous
nerve and vein. Deeper dissection involves retraction of the medial head of the
gastrocnemius and semimembranosus posteriorly.
Posterolateral dissection involves the interval between the iliotibial band and the
anterior border of the biceps femoris. The common peroneal nerve will be protected
posterior to the biceps tendon and distally as it curls around the fibular neck. Palpation
of the nerve during the procedure can reassure the surgical team that it has been
protected throughout the procedure. Deeper dissection proceeds anterior the lateral
head of the gastrocnemius but posterior to the lateral joint capsule.

Surgical Fixation
Fixation methods (Videos 4 and 5)
Inside-out repair technique is the preferred technique.
All-inside devices are increasingly common given their ease of use. More recent studies show
outcomes similar to those of inside-out repair.
Outside-in technique may be useful for anterior horn repair or management of anterior
instability of a discoid lateral meniscus.
Meniscal root repair techniques that involve the use of drill tunnels that exit at the meniscal
root insertion and metaphyseal fixation that involves the use of bone bridge knots, button
fixation, or suture anchor fixation aid in the management of root tears.15

Surgical Fixation
Surgical fixation methods for meniscal tears in pediatric/adolescent patients depend on
the meniscal tear pattern, the presence of discoid morphology, the chronicity of the tear,
the size and age of the patient, and surgeon preference and comfort level with the
available techniques.
Inside-out repair generally is considered the preferred treatment option for peripheral
meniscal repair, particularly for bucket-handle tear patterns (Figure 4); however, all-
inside devices are increasingly common in combination with inside-out repair or as a
stand-alone fixation method given their ease of use. Recent studies show outcomes
similar to those of inside-out repair. Meniscal root repair techniques that involve the use
of drill tunnels that exit at the meniscal root insertion and metaphyseal fixation that
involves the use of bone bridge knots, button fixation, or suture anchor fixation aid in
the management of root tears. Additional techniques also may be used for specific
patterns; the outside-in technique may be useful for anterior horn repair and side-to-
side repair techniques may be useful for radial tears (Figure 5) or the equivalent of a
meniscal root tear.

Postoperative Management
Patients who undergo partial meniscectomy are allowed to bear weight as tolerated
immediately postoperatively.
In general, limited/protected–weight bearing is recommended for 4 to 6 weeks after meniscal
repair to limit compressive forces on the healing tissue.
Range of motion should be limited (ie, 0° to 90° of knee flexion) to avoid shear forces on the
meniscus, tensile forces on the anterior horn, and compressive forces on the posterior horn.
After weight bearing and motion are allowed and restored, rehabilitation will focus on
restoration of strength and sport-specific training for athletes planning to return to sports and
activities.

Postoperative Management
Postoperative rehabilitation after surgical management of meniscal tears in pediatric
and adolescent patients may vary based on the meniscal tear pattern, surgical repair
technique, and patient-specific factors. Patients who undergo partial meniscectomy or
saucerization generally are allowed to bear weight as tolerated immediately

meniscus, tensile forces on the anterior horn, and compressive forces on the posterior
horn; however, some evidence shows that limited–weight bearing and range of motion
postoperatively may not necessarily improve outcomes after meniscal repair. After
weight bearing and motion are allowed and restored, rehabilitation focuses on
restoration of strength and sport-specific training for athletes planning to return to
sports and activities. In general, pediatric/adolescent athletes return to sports 3 to 6
months after isolated meniscal repair.
Complications
17% of surgical procedures for the management of discoid meniscus result in complications
and 13% of surgical procedures for the management of discoid meniscus necessitate revision
surgery.6
Specific complications include the following:
Arthrofibrosis
Retear or propagation of new tear from repair site
Iatrogenic cartilage damage during repair
Degenerative/arthritic changes—Associated with failed meniscal repair or subtotal/total
meniscal loss. These changes can be rapid in the patients with near/complete meniscal loss
(Video 6).

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Saphenous nerve injuries have been reported after inside-out medial meniscus repair and
after all-inside medial meniscus repair.
The common peroneal nerve can be injured during all-inside and inside-out lateral meniscus
repair.
The tibial nerve can be injured during posterior lateral meniscus repairs, particularly with all-
inside devices.16
Rehabilitation
Early physical therapy for range of motion, quadriceps activation, swelling, and pain control
For a repaired meniscus, 4 to 6 weeks of restricted weight bearing and range of motion from
0° to 90°, depending on the size and location of the tear
For meniscectomy, weight bearing as tolerated and no range of motion restrictions

Reported healing rates between 33.3% and 100% and revision surgery rates between 9% and
37%. Concurrent ACL reconstruction may result in improved meniscal repair healing rates.
Better midterm and long-term outcomes of discoid meniscus saucerization are observed in
patients in whom 10 mm of meniscal width is preserved.14
Revision surgery rates may be higher in the surgically managed discoid lateral meniscus
compared with the surgically managed non-discoid meniscus.
Pearls and Pitfalls
A vertical mattress suture pattern has been shown to be the strongest.
Partial meniscectomy is reserved for tears that are irreparable. Given that the potential for
healing is higher in pediatric patients, a more aggressive attempt at repair should be
undertaken.
Marrow venting with the use of an awl or via fine wire drilling in the anterolateral femoral
notch may biologically augment healing of a surgically repaired meniscus.
If using all-inside meniscal repair devices in pediatric knees, the direction and depth of
penetration must be understood to avoid iatrogenic neurovascular injury. The device sheath
often can be shortened to minimize penetration depth.
